item.title: Wisbech street-drinking ban extended by council
item.description:
📰 FENLAND ANGELS RADIO | LOCAL NEWS
Wisbech street-drinking ban extended by council
Fenland District Council has approved an extension to the public space protection order covering Wisbech town centre. The measure, which allows authorities to seize alcohol in areas like Tillery Park and St Peter and Paul Church, was set to expire next week. While 98 per cent of survey respondents supported the renewal, many residents expressed concern that the rules are not being enforced. Councillor Steve Tierney noted that public drinking remains a daily issue, despite police reports indicating a 41 per cent drop in alcohol-related crime since the order was first introduced in 2017. Residents have reported feeling intimidated by the ongoing anti-social behaviour in the town centre.

People living in West Norfolk are being asked to share their views on the future of local health services. Healthwatch Norfolk has launched a public survey to help inform a new clinical strategy for hospitals across the region, including the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in King’s Lynn.
The consultation seeks feedback on current experiences, the delivery of care, and priorities for future generations. Responses will be shared with healthcare professionals and community representatives to help guide long-term planning. Residents can participate in the survey online to ensure their experiences help influence how local NHS services are delivered over the next two decades.

item.title: Historic cobblestones restored at King’s Lynn museum
item.description:
📰 FENLAND ANGELS RADIO | LOCAL NEWS
Historic cobblestones restored at King’s Lynn museum
The first phase of a restoration project at True’s Yard Fisherfolk Museum in King’s Lynn is now complete. Volunteers from the Lynn and West Norfolk Archaeological Society spent two weeks uncovering and restoring original cobblestones in the museum’s courtyard. The historic flooring was discovered after the removal of the Activity vessel, which has since been relocated to Dersingham.
The work has revealed the thresholds of previously demolished cottages, offering a glimpse into the lives of local fishing families from a century ago. Museum officials say the project was made possible through grants and private donations. Future plans for the site include building replica cottages for educational use, an initiative estimated to cost £500,000.
🔗 More details: https://www.lynnnews.co.uk/news/go-back-100-years-in-time-as-cobblestones-as-fisherfolk-muse-9482782/
